content: Please inform your healthcare provider if you experience any side effects from topical gentamicin that are bothersome to you. Common side effects include skin redness, itching, and irritation. There may be other side effects not listed here. If you suspect you are experiencing a side effect, contact your healthcare provider or report it to the FDA at 800-FDA-1088 or Health Canada at 866-234-2345. Serious side effects of topical gentamicin, though less common, can occur. These include severe allergic reactions. Stop using the medication immediately and seek medical attention if you experience symptoms such as difficulty breathing or wheezing, a racing heart, fever or a general feeling of being unwell, swollen lymph nodes, swelling of the face, lips, mouth, tongue, or throat, trouble swallowing or a tight feeling in the throat, itching, skin rash, or hives, nausea or vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. Additionally, using topical gentamicin may lead to secondary infections caused by other organisms, such as fungi. Topical gentamicin should not be used by individuals allergic to gentamicin or any of the ingredients in the specific product. Your pharmacist can provide a complete list of ingredients in the product you are using. Do not use topical gentamicin unless it has been prescribed by a healthcare provider. Use it exactly as directed. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep it out of reach of children. This medication is for external use only and should not be applied to the eyes. If treating impetigo, remove crusts before application to allow the antibiotic to reach the infection. Before using topical gentamicin, inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. This information will help determine if topical gentamicin is appropriate for you. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, discuss this with your healthcare provider, as it is not known if topical gentamicin affects pregnancy or passes into breast milk. There are no known interactions between topical gentamicin and foods or drinks, including alcohol. Additionally, there are no known interactions with other medications. If you or someone else accidentally uses too much topical gentamicin, seek medical help immediately, call 911, or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not use double or extra doses. Complete the full prescribed course of treatment, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of developing antibiotic resistance. Topical gentamicin is an antibiotic used to treat certain bacterial skin infections, such as impetigo or folliculitis. It may also be used for infections associated with skin conditions like eczema or psoriasis, or for infected burns, sores, or wounds. However, its effectiveness may vary depending on the bacteria causing the infection, as some bacteria may have developed resistance to this medication. Your healthcare provider may also prescribe it for other conditions as needed. Topical gentamicin works by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, effectively killing certain types of bacteria. This medication is available as a 1% topical cream or ointment. Store it at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C). It can tolerate short-term exposure to temperatures between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C), such as during transportation.
